newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba approves CNN bureau in Havana.
newsitem.headline: Cuba approves CNN bureau in Havana.

text.p: The Cuban government said on Thursday it approved the opening of a bureau in Havana by U.S. television news company Cable News Network (CNN).
The decision means CNN will become the first U.S. news organisation in decades to be allowed to have a corespondent in the Cuban capital.

"Approval has been given for the establishing of a CNN correspondent in Havana and at this moment the processes for the execution of this decision are being analysed," Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Marianela Ferriol said in a statement.

A spokesman for CNN in Atlanta said the Time Warner Inc. news subsidiary, in view of the ongoing U.S. economic embargo, would await permission from the U.S. government before opening operations on the communist-run island.
CNN informally sought Cuban government approval more than a year ago, and applied to the U.S. Treasury Department for permission last March.
The 24-hour cable news channel was privately notified of the Cuban decision in August and has since sought to expedite matters with the U.S. Treasury and State departments.
"With U.S. sanctions against Cuba, we still await U.S. government approval," said CNN spokesman Steve Haworth.
"We choose to be optimistic. But we have not had any indications yet from the (U.S.) government as to when they may or may not approve the request."
U.S. news organisations such as UPI, AP and the New York Times were closed down in Cuba in the 1960s after Washington enforced an embargo against the revolutionary government led by Fidel Castro.
Cuban authorities, however, permit journalists from U.S. news organisations to pay visits to the island.

Ferriol said the decision was not a blanket authorisation to all news organisations to open offices. Several U.S. news organisations have pending requests to be able to open bureaux in the Cuban capital.
"Other requests remain under study," Ferriol said.
She added that the request from CNN had been granted in the light of "cordial and respectful relations" between the Cuban authorities and CNN.

CNN president Ted Turner has met President Fidel Castro on several occasions in recent years. The network has been active in Cuba in the last several years, with frequent coverage by a correspondent without officially having a bureau in Havana.

President Bill Clinton announced in October 1995 that Washington sought closer people-to-people contact with Cuba despite the longstanding U.S. economic embargo against the island. He said moves to achieve this would include allowing U.S. news organisations to set up bureaux in Cuba.
But this also depended on Cuba giving its authorisation.

Despite the Cuban announcement, it was not clear whether there would be obstacles to CNN opening a bureau under new legislation tightening the embargo approved by Clinton last March, the Helms-Burton law.

The law allows the President to authorise the exchange of news bureaux with Cuba as long as it is fully reciprocal, and if the Cuban government agrees not to interfere with the establishment of bureaux from any U.S.-based news groups, including Radio Marti and Television Marti.

Cuba is unlikely to grant all U.S. news organisations the right to set up bureaux, especially U.S.-government funded media like Radio and Television Marti, which are viewed in Havana as completely hostile to the Castro government.
Officials at the U.S. Interests Section in Havana were not immediately available for comment.
